description: We're Elara, four female engineering students (3 software, 1 electrical) with skills in AI, voice-over, acting, and presenting. We want to turn NASA's open data into something people can explore and enjoy.
summary:
Moono is an interactive film-game for children aged 7–12 that turns them into members of a real Moon mission. Players grow up through three childhood choices, then pick one of five space majors: space-weather scientist, power engineer, space doctor, space farmer or comms engineer. Next they must keep a lunar base alive through a solar storm by balancing three meters: Power, Air and Shield. Every choice has a cost, so kids learn the real trade-offs astronauts face between life support, radiation shielding, power and food.

Every storm in Moono really happened. Flares, particle events and warning times come from NASA's DONKI data. Radiation comes from NASA OSDR RadLab, and space-farming facts come from the Canadian Space Agency's food toolkit and NASA OSDR plant studies. For example, a real X5.1 flare on 11 November 2025 gave astronauts only 31 minutes of warning.

Moono matters because the path to space is now open: Saudi astronauts flew in 2023. Yet most children still can't see that path. Moono shows them that any major has a place in space, at their level and in five minutes. It runs on any phone with no install, and it collects no data.
details: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational game designed to inspire children and young people to explore space science and discover careers in space exploration. Players begin by making childhood choices that shape their future astronaut specialization. They then participate in a lunar mission where they must protect their crew and base during a real historical solar storm by managing three essential resources: electrical power, breathable air, and radiation shielding. The game uses historical solar storm data from NASA, including solar flares, energetic particle events, and coronal mass ejections, to create realistic mission scenarios. Its main benefits are promoting STEM education, increasing awareness of space-related careers, and developing critical thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making skills. The project's creativity lies in combining real NASA scientific data, career exploration, interactive storytelling, and resource management into an engaging gaming experience. It was developed as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with GitHub Pages for hosting. NASA's DONKI database and other scientific resources, including NASA OSDR RadLab and NTRS, supported the scientific content. AI-assisted tools were also used for coding support and voice narration. During development, the team considered scientific accuracy, age appropriateness, accessibility, and user engagement, ensuring that complex scientific concepts could be understood by younger audiences. Ultimately, the project aims to transform real space science into an enjoyable learning experience that inspires the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space explorers.
